findings.title: Dummy hash is rebuilt every request, inverting the timing cover (user enumeration)
findings.evidence: dummyHash caches with a function static: '    static $hash = null;' and builds the hash with password_hash(bin2hex(random_bytes(16)), PASSWORD_DEFAULT). PHP function statics do not persist between requests (fresh engine state per request in PHP-FPM/mod_php), so every attemptLogin call with an unknown email executes one full password_hash plus one password_verify, while a known email executes only one password_verify.
findings.recommendation: Replace the generated dummy hash with a precomputed constant PHC string (e.g. a hard-coded '$2y$10$...' bcrypt hash of a random throwaway value with the same cost/options used by registerUser), so both branches perform exactly one verify and the cost is identical.

findings.title: No maximum password length: bcrypt truncates at 72 bytes so distinct long passwords verify identically
findings.evidence: registerUser only enforces a lower bound (strlen < 12 throws) and then calls '    $hash = password_hash($password, PASSWORD_DEFAULT);'. With PASSWORD_DEFAULT (bcrypt) PHP silently truncates input at 72 bytes, so a caller registered with a 200-byte password will also authenticate with any other 200-byte password sharing the first 72 bytes; attemptLogin calls password_verify on the same truncated material.
findings.recommendation: Reject passwords longer than 72 bytes at registration (and do not rely on silent truncation), or pre-hash with a strong digest before bcrypt, or use PASSWORD_ARGON2ID which has no such truncation.

findings.title: Length rule counts bytes but the error message claims characters
findings.evidence: '    if (strlen($password) < 12) {' counts bytes while the thrown message says password must be at least 12 characters, so a 6-character multibyte (UTF-8) password passes the policy sized in characters.
findings.recommendation: Either use mb_strlen($password, 'UTF-8') if the policy is character based, or reword the error to state bytes and document the byte-based cap.

findings.title: strict_types turns a NULL/absent password_hash into a TypeError instead of a generic failure
findings.evidence: With declare(strict_types=1) in this file, a NULL column value is not coerced: '    $passwordOk = password_verify($password, $hash);' throws TypeError when users.password_hash is NULL (e.g. rows created by SSO/invite flows), producing a 500 instead of the single generic null return. Depends on the schema allowing NULL, which this diff does not show.
findings.recommendation: Guard the stored hash: treat a non-string or empty password_hash as an always-fail credential and route it through the dummy-hash timing path instead of passing NULL to password_verify.

findings.title: Duplicate email surfaces as an unhandled PDOException (and an account-existence oracle)
findings.evidence: '    $stmt->execute(['email' => $email, 'hash' => $hash]);' has no duplicate handling; a second registration for the same email hits the unique constraint and propagates an uncaught exception, which both returns a 500 on a normal user action and tells the caller whether the account already exists, bypassing the deliberately generic login failure.
findings.recommendation: Catch the unique-constraint violation and map it to a defined domain error (or run the insert as an upsert/INSERT IGNORE where appropriate), so duplicate registration never leaks a stack trace or a distinguishable outcome.
